issue: Request bodies are not validated with @Valid
explanation: The createIncident and updateStatus endpoints accept @RequestBody DTOs without the @Valid annotation. This means any Bean Validation annotations (e.g., @NotNull, @Size, @NotBlank) on IncidentRequestDTO and IncidentStatusUpdateRequestDTO are skipped, allowing malformed/invalid payloads to reach the service layer and possibly the database.
fix: Add @Valid before @RequestBody, e.g. public ResponseEntity<IncidentResponseDTO> createIncident(@Valid @RequestBody IncidentRequestDTO requestDTO) { ... } and similarly for updateStatus. Also ensure the DTOs are annotated with constraints like @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size.
recommendation: Always validate inbound DTOs at the controller boundary and handle MethodArgumentNotValidException with a @ControllerAdvice to return structured 400 responses.
insights: Centralizing validation prevents leakage of invalid state into the service and persistence layers, reducing the chance of constraint exceptions surfacing late.

explanation: Routes mix camelCase (/calculatedSeverity/...), uppercase literals (/CRITICAL), and lowercase (/status/...). REST URL conventions recommend lowercase, kebab-case paths. Inconsistency makes the API harder to discover and maintain, and uppercase path segments can be confusing because URIs are case-sensitive.
fix: Rename paths to use lowercase kebab-case: /calculated-severity/{calculatedSeverity}, /critical, /admin/calculated-severity/{calculatedSeverity}, /admin/critical, /admin/open-department, etc.
recommendation: Adopt a consistent URL style guide (kebab-case, lowercase, plural nouns) across the entire API and document it.
insights: Consistent URL naming improves client developer experience and reduces routing bugs when generating OpenAPI clients.

explanation: @GetMapping("/CRITICAL") and @GetMapping("/{incidentId}") both match /api/incidents/CRITICAL. Spring resolves more specific patterns first so /CRITICAL wins here, but if a client passes a non-numeric path variable that happens to be 'admin' or any literal in the future, route conflicts and conversion errors can occur. Likewise /admin and /{incidentId} share the same prefix and rely on the Long type conversion failing for non-numeric paths.
fix: Either constrain the path variable with regex, e.g. @GetMapping("/{incidentId:\\d+}"), or move literal endpoints under a clearly distinct prefix like /by-id/{incidentId} and /filter/critical to remove ambiguity.
recommendation: Use path-variable regex constraints or distinct sub-paths to eliminate any route ambiguity between literal endpoints and dynamic IDs.
insights: Explicit constraints make routes self-documenting and prevent surprising 404s/400s due to type-conversion failures.

issue: Misleading variable naming (incidents for single object)
explanation: In getIncidentDetails, withdrawIncident, and updateStatus, the single IncidentResponseDTO is assigned to a variable named 'incidents' (plural). This reduces readability and can mislead future maintainers.
fix: Rename to 'incident' (singular), e.g. IncidentResponseDTO incident = incidentService.getIncidentDetails(incidentId); return ResponseEntity.ok(incident);
recommendation: Use names that accurately reflect the cardinality and intent of the variable.
insights: Small naming improvements significantly aid long-term maintainability and code reviews.

issue: Withdraw endpoint uses PUT but represents a state change action
explanation: /withdraw/{incidentId} uses PUT without a request body. PUT semantically means full replacement of a resource. A state transition action is better modeled as POST /{incidentId}/withdraw, or PATCH /{incidentId} with a status field. Additionally, the path puts the action before the ID, which is inconsistent with /{incidentId}/status used later.
fix: Change to @PostMapping("/{incidentId}/withdraw") or @PatchMapping("/{incidentId}") for consistency, e.g. @PostMapping("/{incidentId}/withdraw") public ResponseEntity<IncidentResponseDTO> withdrawIncident(@PathVariable Long incidentId) { ... }
recommendation: Follow REST conventions: POST for non-idempotent actions/state transitions, PATCH for partial updates, PUT for full replacement.
insights: Consistent resource/action URL structure improves API predictability for clients.

explanation: CrossOrigin is imported but not used. If a frontend depends on cross-origin calls, this controller will fail without a global CORS configuration. Conversely, leaving the import dead is sloppy.
fix: Remove the unused import: delete 'import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.CrossOrigin;'. Configure CORS globally via WebMvcConfigurer addCorsMappings or in Spring Security configuration rather than per-controller annotations.
recommendation: Centralize CORS configuration in one place (security or WebMvc config) to ensure consistency across all controllers.
insights: Unused imports are flagged by static analyzers; cleaning them up keeps the codebase tidy and reviewable.

issue: No global exception handling visible / inconsistent error responses
explanation: Controller endpoints rely on the service layer throwing exceptions (e.g., for not-found, access-denied incidents) but there is no @ControllerAdvice referenced. Without one, clients may receive generic 500 errors with stack traces, leaking internal details.
fix: Add a @RestControllerAdvice class that maps domain exceptions to ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> with appropriate HTTP statuses (404, 403, 400, etc.) and a uniform error payload schema.
recommendation: Centralize exception-to-HTTP mapping via @RestControllerAdvice and never expose stack traces to clients.
insights: A consistent error contract simplifies client error handling and aids observability/log correlation.

issue: List endpoints return unbounded collections (no pagination)
explanation: All GET endpoints returning List<IncidentResponseDTO> can return arbitrarily large result sets (especially /admin and /admin/status/{status}). This can cause performance issues, large memory consumption, and slow responses as data grows.
fix: Switch to Pageable: e.g. public ResponseEntity<Page<IncidentResponseDTO>> getAllIncidentsForAdmin(Pageable pageable) { return ResponseEntity.ok(incidentService.getAllIncidents(pageable)); } and update repositories/services to accept Pageable.
recommendation: Always paginate list endpoints; add sort and filter query parameters for flexibility.
insights: Pagination, sorting, and filtering should be designed in early; retrofitting them later often breaks API contracts.

issue: Enum path variables not validated for invalid values
explanation: Endpoints accept IncidentStatus and IncidentSeverity directly as path variables. If a client passes an unknown value, Spring will return a 400 with a default Spring error or even a 500 depending on configuration. There is no graceful handling or documented allowed values.
fix: Either keep the enum binding and add a handler for MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException in @ControllerAdvice to return a clear 400 with allowed values, or accept a String and validate manually with a helpful error message.
recommendation: Provide explicit, friendly error messages listing valid enum values and document them in OpenAPI.
insights: Better client error responses reduce support overhead and improve developer experience.

issue: Use of @PostMapping() and @GetMapping() with empty parentheses
explanation: Minor stylistic issue: @PostMapping() and @GetMapping() with empty parentheses are equivalent to @PostMapping and @GetMapping without parentheses. Inconsistent style across the codebase reduces readability.
recommendation: Adopt a consistent annotation style and enforce with a formatter/checkstyle rule.
insights: Style consistency, enforced by automated tooling, reduces noise in diffs and reviews.
